analysis.one_liner: Transfers most federal public lands in every state to state ownership, capping federal landholding at 20 percent per state.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote and died in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, with no cosponsors, when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, introduced in the final month of a two-year Congress, would have automatically handed nearly all land owned by the federal government over to the states starting in 1998, except for national parks, Indian trust lands, and up to 20 percent of each state's acreage that a president could keep. States that felt the president kept too much could sue, and a judge would have to trim the federal list using only a priority list the governor provided, with no further review. The federal government would stay on the hook for cleanup costs on any contaminated land it transferred.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries that use or want access to public land — mining, timber, grazing, and energy companies — would gain the most, because state control generally makes it easier and cheaper to get permits for development than federal management does. State governments would gain title to enormous acreage, and the federal Treasury would shed the cost of managing it. Anyone wanting weaker environmental oversight on former federal land would benefit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Mining, timber, grazing, and energy interests

how_it_helps.text: All federal real property that was ever part of the public domain would automatically vest in the states on January 1, 1998, subject only to a few exclusions and valid existing rights.

National Park System lands, lands held in trust for federally recognized Indian tribes and their members, lands a governor declines, and up to 20 percent of a state's acreage chosen by the president would be excluded from the transfer.

If the president's retention list exceeded 20 percent of a state's acreage, the governor could sue in federal court, and the judge would be required to trim the list using only the governor's own priority list, which would be final and unreviewable.
The federal government would remain strictly liable for hazardous-material cleanup on land it transferred, keeping cleanup costs off the states' books.
The bill states its purposes as improving public land management, reducing federal expenditures, and empowering states over former public-domain lands.

analysis.who_pays: The general public. Federal lands are managed for all Americans, including hunters, anglers, hikers, and campers; state ownership could open the door to sale, leasing, or development that limits or fees public access, and state budgets and wildlife and environmental rules would bear the management burden instead of a national one. The federal government would also keep paying cleanup costs on contaminated transferred land.
analysis.who_pays_short: All Americans who use public lands

drawbacks.text: Transferring lands held in common for the whole country to individual states could restrict access for hunting, fishing, grazing, and recreation, since states could sell, lease, or manage the land under their own rules with no national duty to keep it open to everyone.
State and local governments would absorb the cost of managing vast acreage, including roads, firefighting, and wildlife programs, without any accompanying federal payment.

The governor's priority list for forcing land out of federal retention would be final and immune from review, giving a single state official decisive say over which federal facilities stay — an unusual amount of power over national assets like military bases or research sites.

Because the federal government would remain strictly liable for hazardous-waste cleanup on transferred land, taxpayers nationwide could still pay for contamination problems on land the government no longer controls.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: States would acquire valuable land and the federal Treasury would save management costs, but the bill's structure — automatic transfer, an unreviewable gubernatorial priority list, and no requirement that states keep the land open to the public — pointed toward development over public access. Its costs to Americans who use public lands, and to federal taxpayers still on the hook for cleanup, were substantial and largely uncompensated.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with about a month left in the Congress, referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and never heard from again — no hearing, no vote, no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Sen. Malcolm Wallop introduced the bill on December 1, 1994, in the final month of the 103rd Congress.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day.
No cosponsors ever joined, and no further committee or floor action occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary Americans who hunt, fish, hike, and camp on federal public land, and national conservation interests, since the lands stayed under federal ownership and management.

for.name: Sen. Malcolm Wallop
for.role: U.S. Senator from Wyoming; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Public Land Emancipation and Management Improvement Act and delivered introductory remarks on the floor.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Bennett Johnston
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — during the final month of the Congress.

against.name: No Senate cosponsors
against.role: Every other member of the 100-seat Senate
against.what_they_did: Declined to sign on to the bill during its one month of life, leaving it with zero cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the bill's partisan shape beyond its lone Republican sponsor cannot be measured.

industries.industry: Mining, timber, grazing, and energy interests
industries.note: State control of former federal land generally makes permitting for mining, logging, grazing, and drilling easier and cheaper, and states could sell or lease the land. The public cost is potential loss of access and weaker environmental rules on land now owned by everyone.

Hunters, anglers, hikers, and campers use federal land under national access guarantees; transfer to states could bring sales, leases, or fees that limit access. Their loss would be the flip side of industry's gain.
States would gain title to enormous acreage and control over it, but would also absorb the full cost of managing it — roads, firefighting, wildlife — with no federal payment.

industries.industry: Federal land management agencies (Forest Service, Bureau of Land Management)
industries.note: The bill's stated purpose includes reducing federal spending on public lands, which would shrink the agencies' portfolios and budgets, though savings would come at the cost of national stewardship of shared lands.
